newsitem.title: THAILAND: New loans for Thailand still on cards - Japan banks.
newsitem.headline: New loans for Thailand still on cards - Japan banks.

text.p: Japanese bank officials in Bangkok said on Wednesday private-sector rescue loans for Thailand were still on the cards, although Thai authorities did not request new money at their Tokyo meeting on Tuesday.
Thai monetary authorities urged representatives of 21 major Japanese commercial banks on Tuesday to continue supporting the country by rolling over existing loans.
The meeting came a day after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Asian neighbours unveiled their larger-than-expected $16 billion rescue loan package for Thailand worth $16 billion.

"It was not clear whether Thailand did not ask for new loans in the belief that the time was not ripe to do so or because they think the public-sector rescue loans will be enough," said a senior official at a leading Japanese bank in Bangkok.
"But I think private-sector rescue measures are still likely to be discussed...probably after the IMF's formal approval of the rescue loan scheme on August 21," the official said.

Japanese banks were generally positive about rolling over their existing loans to Thai firms. But they said they needed to take a case-by-case approach, depending on the financial conditions of each Thai firm involved, bank officials said.

Thailand has nearly $89 billion in foreign currency debt, with Japanese banks accounting for nearly half of it. There had been talk private banks from Japan and other nations may be preparing to shoulder a total burden of some $5 billion.
Another Japanese bank official here said the IMF loan package was "a big step forward" in healing Thailand's economic pains.
"But when it comes to whether this will be enough to cure the economic illness, nobody knows," he said.

Japanese bankers said they needed more time to further estimate foreign capital outflows from the country, particularly since some creditor banks would be hesitant to rollover exsisting loans due to Thailand's deteriorating financial health.
The IMF loan package was designed to plug holes in foreign reserves created when Bangkok floated its baht currency last month after failing to defend the currency from speculative attacks.
But how Thailand will save its troubled financial sector, where about two thirds of finance firms have been ordered to suspend operations, remains unclear.
Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said on Wednesday the 58 suspended finance firms would take six to eight months to reform through mergers among themselves or with stronger firms.

Thai authorities have assured Japanese bankers Bangkok will guarantee the principal of foreign loans to the newly suspended 42 financial firms but said interests on the loans could fall, a Japanese banking source said in Tokyo.
The first Japanese bank official said it would not be surprising if the Thai government asked creditors to cut interest requirements on loans to Thai firms.

"It's possible for the country's credit ratings to be downgraded, then borrowing conditions should get worse. It would be no wonder for the Thai government to ask creditors to stop any increase in interest rates, or even redure," he said. -- Bangkok newsroom (662)-6520642 --email: bangkok.newsroom@reuters.com
